warmup.q: A request coroutine calls GlobalScope.launch { refund(id) } and then the client disconnects, so the request coroutine is cancelled. What happens to the refund?
options: It is cancelled too, because it was started from the request
It keeps running: it belongs to GlobalScope, not to the request
It is paused until the request is retried
The JVM throws IllegalStateException when the request is cancelled
warmup.why: Cancellation travels down a tree of parent and child jobs. GlobalScope has no job, so a coroutine launched there has no parent. The request being cancelled does not reach it, nobody waits for it, and nobody hears about its failure.

sections.h: Every coroutine has a parent, and a parent waits for its children
sections.html:
Every coroutine you start with launch or async gets a Job, and that job becomes a child of the job in the scope you called it on. Children can have children. The result is a tree, and the tree is the whole idea behind structured concurrency: concurrent work has the same nested shape as the code that started it.

Java
// Java equivalent: nested StructuredTaskScope (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505; needs --enable-preview)
try (var details = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {      // a node, like coroutineScope
    details.fork(() -> accounts.load(id));
    details.fork(() -> ledger.recent(id, 20));
    details.fork(() -> risk.flags(id));
    details.join();                                     // waits for all three subtasks
}
Kotlin
runBlocking(CoroutineName("request")) {          // root
    launch(CoroutineName("details")) {             // child of request
        coroutineScope {                           // a node of its own
            async(CoroutineName("account")) { /* ... */ }
            async(CoroutineName("ledger")) { /* ... */ }
            launch(CoroutineName("risk")) { /* ... */ }
        }
    }
}

A scope is just a coroutine context that holds a job. The context is the small set of settings that travels with a coroutine: its job, its name, its dispatcher. Lesson 4 of this track takes it apart. launch reads the job from the scope's context and attaches the new coroutine to it. coroutineScope adds a node of its own between its caller and the children started inside it.

The first rule of the tree: a parent cannot complete until all of its children have completed. When the body of a coroutine finishes, its job enters a waiting state ("completing") until every child is done. That is why coroutineScope returns only after the slowest child, and why runBlocking doesn't return while anything below it is still running. Completed children leave the tree, so job.children lists only the work that is still going.

The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 docs spell out four rules for how lifecycles interact. The parent waits for its children. Cancelling the parent cancels the children. A child that fails with an exception cancels its parent (unless the parent is a supervisor, lesson 6 of this track). And a child that ends with CancellationException counts as cancelled, so the parent is not told. The next section is about the middle two.

try.title: Print the tree
steps: Read JobTree.kt. Before running it, sketch the tree you expect to see at 100 ms, with names.
Run it and compare with your sketch.
Why does details appear twice? (Hint: what does coroutineScope inherit from its parent?)

code.title: JobTree.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Job import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.job import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Prints a Job and all of its children, indented. */ fun Job.printTree(indent: String = "") { // every coroutine is also a CoroutineScope, so we can read the name from its context val name = (this as? CoroutineScope)?.coroutineContext?.get(CoroutineName)?.name ?: "(coroutineScope)" println("$indent$name active=$isActive children=${children.count()}") children.forEach { it.printTree("$indent ") } } fun main() = runBlocking(CoroutineName("request")) { val details = launch(CoroutineName("details")) { coroutineScope { async(CoroutineName("account")) { delay(300) } async(CoroutineName("ledger")) { delay(300) } launch(CoroutineName("risk")) { delay(300) } delay(100) // give the children time to start println("tree at 100 ms, seen from the request coroutine:") this@runBlocking.coroutineContext.job.printTree() } } details.join() println("after join: request has ${coroutineContext.job.children.count()} children") }

try.expect: request has one child, details. Under it sits a second node also called details: that is the coroutineScope, which inherits its parent's context, name included. It has three children: account, ledger and risk. After join, the request has 0 children, because finished children leave the tree.

sections.h: Failure goes up, cancellation goes down
sections.html:
Take the payment details endpoint from lesson 2 of this track: account, ledger and risk calls as three children of one coroutineScope. The ledger call throws IOException at 100 ms. Here is what the tree does, in order:

  1. The ledger child fails. It reports the exception to its parent, the scope.
  2. The scope's job is cancelled with that exception. A cancelled job cancels all of its children, so the account and risk calls are cancelled. Their finally blocks run.
  3. The scope waits until those children have actually stopped.
  4. coroutineScope rethrows the IOException to its caller, which can catch it like any exception.

So a single failure takes down the whole subtree it belongs to, and then surfaces as one exception at the place that started the work. The total time is the time to the failure, about 100 ms, not the time of the slowest call. Nothing is left running in the background holding a connection.

Cancellation only travels down. If the caller cancels the request (the client hung up, or a timeout fired), every coroutine below it is cancelled. A child that is cancelled does not cancel its parent. A child whose block ends by throwing CancellationException is treated the same way: it is "cancelled", not "failed", and the parent carries on.

This is the default because it is almost always what a request needs. If one of three calls needed to build the response has failed, there is no response, so the other two calls are wasted work. When you do want siblings to survive each other's failures (sending a notification to email, SMS and push), you ask for it explicitly with a supervisor. That is lesson 6 of this track.

One caution from the docs: cancellation reaches a coroutine only at a suspension point. A child stuck in a CPU loop or a blocking call finishes that first. Lesson 5 of this track shows how to cooperate.

try.title: Watch one failure take down a scope
steps: Read FailureSpreads.kt. Predict which lines print, and at roughly what times.
Run it with -Pargs=ok, so the ledger does not fail. Predict when coroutineScope returns.
Run the Java twin, then run it with -Pargs=cancel. Compare what happens to the risk task.

code.title: FailureSpreads.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException /** One child fails at 100 ms. Watch what happens to its sibling and to the caller. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val ledgerFails = args.firstOrNull() != "ok" val t0 = System.nanoTime() fun log(msg: String) = println("[%4d ms] %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg)) try { coroutineScope { launch { delay(100) if (ledgerFails) { log("ledger: throwing IOException") throw IOException("ledger unavailable") } log("ledger: done") } launch { try { delay(1_000) log("risk: done") } finally { log("risk: finally block runs") } } log("scope body finished; the scope now waits for its children") } log("coroutineScope returned normally") } catch (e: IOException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: FailureSpreadsJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FailureSpreads.kt with a virtual-thread executor (JDK 21+, no preview APIs). // An executor has no parent-child tree: a failed task does not cancel its sibling unless you do it. // Pass "cancel" to cancel the sibling by hand, which is what coroutineScope does for you. package workbench.coroutines.l03; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; public class FailureSpreadsJava { static long t0; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("[%4d ms] %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean cancelByHand = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService children = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<?> ledger = children.submit(() -> { sleep(100); log("ledger: throwing IOException"); throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("ledger unavailable")); }); Future<?> risk = children.submit(() -> { try { sleep(1_000); log("risk: done"); } finally { log("risk: finally block runs"); } }); try { ledger.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("caller caught: " + e.getCause().getCause().getMessage()); if (cancelByHand) risk.cancel(true); // interrupts the sibling } } // close() waits for every task, including the sibling nobody cancelled log("executor closed"); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException("interrupted", e); } } }

try.expect: The scope body finishes first, at a few ms. At about 100 ms the ledger throws, and within a few ms the risk child's finally runs and the caller catches ledger unavailable. risk: done never prints. (The first delay can read 150 ms or so on a cold JVM.) With -Pargs=ok, coroutineScope returns at about 1,000 ms, after the slowest child. The Java twin is the honest contrast: an executor has no tree, so after the ledger fails the risk task runs to risk: done at about 1,000 ms, and close() waits for it. With -Pargs=cancel you cancel the sibling by hand and its finally runs at about 100 ms (the last two lines can come in either order). coroutineScope does that step for you.

sections.h: GlobalScope cuts work loose from the tree
sections.html:
GlobalScope is a scope with no job. A coroutine launched in it has no parent, so none of the rules above apply. Nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it, and its exception goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler, which usually means a log line nobody reads.

Java
// Java equivalent: a task on a shared, app-wide pool; nothing ties it to the request
void startRefund(String id) {
    SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> refundSteps(id));   // returns at once; the refund is an orphan
}
Kotlin
suspend fun startRefund(id: String) {
    GlobalScope.launch { refundSteps(id) }   // returns at once; the refund is an orphan
}

The caller of startRefund thinks the refund is part of its request. It is not. When the client gives up and the request coroutine is cancelled, the refund keeps going. In a test, it keeps running after the test has finished and may fail the next one. At shutdown, it can still be writing when the connection pool closes. This is a leaked coroutine: work that outlives everything that knows about it.

kotlinx.coroutines marks GlobalScope as @DelicateCoroutinesApi, so you have to opt in, and its docs call using it an antipattern. They also warn about the obvious workaround: CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { } inside a function creates a brand-new root scope on every call and has every one of the same problems. The opt-in warning just doesn't fire.

The fix depends on what you meant. If the caller should wait for the refund, call it directly, or use coroutineScope { launch { } } when it runs alongside other work. If the refund really should outlive the request, then something with a longer life has to own it: a component with its own scope, which the next section builds. In payments it often means something else again: write the refund to an outbox table or a Temporal workflow, so it survives a restart. An in-memory coroutine doesn't.

There is one legitimate use: a coroutine that lives exactly as long as the whole application, such as a metrics reporter started in main.

try.title: Cancel a request and watch the refund carry on
steps: Read LeakedWork.kt. The request is cancelled at 250 ms. Predict how many refund steps print after that.
Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which uses the coroutineScope version. Predict first.
Run the Java twin both ways. It interrupts a request thread instead of cancelling a coroutine.

code.title: LeakedWork.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.DelicateCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.GlobalScope import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var start = 0L private fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 private suspend fun refundSteps(id: String) { repeat(6) { step -> delay(100) println(" [${ms()} ms] refund $id: step $step") } } /** Leaks: the refund belongs to GlobalScope, not to the request that started it. */ @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun startRefundLeaky(id: String) { GlobalScope.launch { refundSteps(id) } } /** Structured: the refund is a child of the caller. */ suspend fun startRefund(id: String) = coroutineScope { launch { refundSteps(id) } } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val structured = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" start = System.nanoTime() val request = launch { if (structured) startRefund("r-17") else startRefundLeaky("r-17") delay(10_000) // the request goes on to do other things } delay(250) request.cancel() println("[${ms()} ms] request cancelled (client gave up)") delay(500) // keep the JVM alive a little to see what still runs println("[${ms()} ms] main done") }

alt.title: LeakedWorkJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of LeakedWork.kt: a request thread hands the refund to a shared pool. // Interrupting the request (the client gave up) does not reach the pool's task. // Pass "fixed" to run the refund in the request's own thread, so the interrupt stops it. package workbench.coroutines.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class LeakedWorkJava { static final ExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(r -> { // lives as long as the app Thread t = new Thread(r, "shared-pool"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; }); static long start; static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; } static void refundSteps(String id) throws InterruptedException { for (int step = 0; step < 6; step++) { Thread.sleep(100); System.out.printf(" [%d ms] refund %s: step %d%n", ms(), id, step); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean structured = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); start = System.nanoTime(); Thread request = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { try { if (structured) refundSteps("r-17"); // part of the request else SHARED.submit(() -> { refundSteps("r-17"); return null; }); // an orphan Thread.sleep(10_000); // the request goes on to other things } catch (InterruptedException e) { // the request was cancelled } }); Thread.sleep(250); request.interrupt(); System.out.printf("[%d ms] request interrupted (client gave up)%n", ms()); Thread.sleep(500); System.out.printf("[%d ms] main done%n", ms()); } }

try.expect: With GlobalScope, steps 2 to 5 keep printing after request cancelled: the refund never heard about it. With -Pargs=fixed, the refund is a child of the request, so nothing prints after request cancelled except main done. The Java twin leaks the same way: interrupting the request thread does not reach a task on a shared pool. Its fixed version runs the refund on the request's own thread, so the interrupt stops it.

refs.title: GlobalScope (API reference: why it is delicate)

sections.h: A class that starts background work owns a scope and closes it
sections.html:
Some work really does outlive a single call: a settler that works through card batches for one Kafka partition, an FX rate refresher, a cache warmer. The structured way to write it is a class that owns a scope, launches into it, and cancels it when its own life ends.

Java
// Java equivalent: the class owns an executor and shuts it down
class BatchSettler implements AutoCloseable {
    private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();   // 1. the class's own pool
    private final Consumer<String> settle;

    BatchSettler(Consumer<String> settle) { this.settle = settle; }

    Future<?> submit(String batchId) {
        return pool.submit(() -> settle.accept(batchId));                               // 2. every batch runs in it
    }

    @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
        pool.shutdownNow();                                                             // 3. interrupt them all
        pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);                                   //    and wait
    }
}
Kotlin
class BatchSettler(context: CoroutineContext, private val settle: suspend (String) -> Unit) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(context + Job())      // 1. the class's own root

    fun submit(batchId: String): Job =
        scope.launch { settle(batchId) }                      // 2. every batch is a child

    suspend fun shutdown() =
        scope.coroutineContext.job.cancelAndJoin()            // 3. cancel them all, wait
}

The scope's job is the parent of every batch. One call to cancel reaches all of them, and job.children tells you what is still running. The tree still exists. Its root is now the object, not a request.

A few rules keep this honest.

Tie the scope to a real lifecycle. Cancel it in @PreDestroy in a Quarkus bean, in onPartitionsRevoked for a Kafka partition worker, or in @AfterEach in a test. An owned scope that nobody cancels is just GlobalScope with extra steps.

Create it once, as a field. A scope created inside a method is the orphan from the previous section.

Pass the dispatcher (or the whole context) in. Production can use Dispatchers.IO, and tests can pass a test dispatcher and run on virtual time. The lab does exactly this.

Choose cancel or cancelAndJoin on purpose. scope.cancel() is not a suspend function and returns at once, while children are still running their finally blocks. cancelAndJoin() waits until they have stopped, which is what you want before closing a connection pool.

CoroutineScope(...) adds a Job() for you if the context has none, but write it out so readers see it. With a plain Job, one failed batch cancels the whole settler. Lesson 6 of this track swaps it for a SupervisorJob, so batches can fail on their own.

Quick check: you call scope.cancel() and close the connection pool on the next line, while three batches still have a finally that returns a connection. What can go wrong, and which one change fixes it? (cancel() returns before those finally blocks have run, so they may hand connections back to a pool that is already closed. cancelAndJoin() waits for them first.)

analogy: A family on a day out. The parent won't leave the park until every child is back at the car. If one child gets hurt, the parent calls everyone back and the trip ends, and the parent then tells whoever is waiting at home what happened. If a child simply decides they've had enough and sits in the car, nobody panics. GlobalScope is a child who wandered off with no parent at all: nobody will look for them at closing time. An owned scope is a school trip: the school, not any one parent, brings everyone home at the end of the day. The analogy breaks on timing. Real children come back when they hear the call. A coroutine only hears it at its next suspension point, so a child busy in a CPU loop keeps going until it pauses.
world: Two places in a payments service need this most. First, request fan-out: a payment details or checkout endpoint that calls three services should do so inside coroutineScope, so a failure or a client disconnect cancels the other calls and releases their Oracle connections. Second, partition-scoped background work in a Kafka consumer. Give each assigned partition a worker with its own scope, launch the per-partition jobs into it, and call shutdown() (cancel and join) in onPartitionsRevoked, before the offsets are committed and the partition moves to another pod. If those jobs ran in GlobalScope, two pods could settle the same batch during a rebalance. Anything that must survive a pod restart belongs in an outbox table or a Temporal workflow, not in a coroutine.
mistake: The most common mistake is reaching for GlobalScope.launch (or CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch inside a function) to "run this in the background" from a request. It compiles and seems to work, so it ships. The cost shows up later: work keeps running after the client has gone, tests interfere with each other, failures only appear as stray log lines, and shutdown races with in-flight writes. Decide who owns the work. If the caller should wait, use coroutineScope. If the work should outlive the call, give a long-lived component a scope it owns and cancels at the end of its life. If it must survive a restart, use durable storage, not a coroutine.

compare.title: Fan-out that cannot leak: StructuredTaskScope vs coroutineScope

java.title: PaymentDetails.java (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505: compile and run with --enable-preview)
java.html: Details details(PaymentId id) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default: fail on the first failure Subtask<Account> account = scope.fork(() -> accounts.load(id)); Subtask<List<Entry>> entries = scope.fork(() -> ledger.recent(id, 20)); scope.join(); // waits; throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException if a subtask failed return new Details(account.get(), entries.get()); } // close() cancels unfinished subtasks and waits for them }

kotlin.title: PaymentDetails.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun details(id: PaymentId): Details = coroutineScope { val account = async { accounts.load(id) } val entries = async { ledger.recent(id, 20) } Details(account.await(), entries.await()) } // returns only when both children are done; a failure cancels the other

compare.note: The idea is the same in both: subtasks cannot outlive the block that started them, the first failure cancels the siblings, and the caller gets one exception. In Java each subtask is a virtual thread running blocking code, and cancellation means interruption. In Kotlin each child is a coroutine, and cancellation reaches it at its next suspension point. The bigger practical difference is maturity. In JDK 25, StructuredTaskScope is a preview API that needs --enable-preview, and its shape has changed between previews (the JDK 21 to 24 previews used a different, subclass-based API). In Kotlin, every launch and async already joins the tree, including calls deep inside other suspend functions, and you get the guarantee without asking for it.

worked.title: Give an FX rate refresher a scope it owns

steps.say: A Quarkus bean refreshes FX rates every 30 seconds. It was written with GlobalScope. After shutdown it keeps calling the rate provider against a closed connection pool, and in tests one instance's loop keeps running into the next test.
steps.code: class FxRateRefresher(private val rates: RateSource) { @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class) fun start() { GlobalScope.launch { while (true) { rates.refresh(); delay(30.seconds) } } } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the bug: a static scheduler that nobody shuts down class FxRateRefresher { private static final ScheduledExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1); private final RateSource rates; void start() { SHARED.scheduleWithFixedDelay(rates::refresh, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

steps.say: Give the class its own scope, created once, with the dispatcher passed in so tests can use a test dispatcher. A CoroutineName makes it easy to spot in thread dumps and debug output.
steps.code: class FxRateRefresher( private val rates: RateSource, dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, ) : AutoCloseable { // 1. one scope per instance; its Job is the parent of everything we start private val scope = CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job() + CoroutineName("fx-refresher"))

alt.html: // Java equivalent: one scheduler per instance, with a named thread class FxRateRefresher implements AutoCloseable { private final RateSource rates; // 1. the instance owns its scheduler private final ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(Thread.ofPlatform().name("fx-refresher").factory());

steps.say: Launch into that scope. Catch failures of a single refresh inside the loop, so one bad response does not end the loop and, with a plain Job, cancel the whole scope. Rethrow CancellationException (lesson 5 of this track explains why).
steps.code: // 2. the loop is a child of the scope fun start(): Job = scope.launch { while (true) { try { rates.refresh() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("rate refresh failed", e) } delay(30.seconds) } }

alt.html: // 2. the refresh belongs to this instance's scheduler ScheduledFuture<?> start() { return scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rates.refresh(); } catch (Exception e) { log.warn("rate refresh failed", e); } // an escaping exception stops the schedule }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); }

steps.say: Close the scope when the owner's life ends: @PreDestroy in the bean, @AfterEach in a test. cancel() returns at once; use cancelAndJoin() from suspend code when you must wait for the loop to stop.
steps.code: // 3. tie the scope to a real lifecycle override fun close() = scope.cancel() } @ApplicationScoped class RatesLifecycle(private val refresher: FxRateRefresher) { @PreDestroy fun stop() = refresher.close() }

alt.html: // 3. tie the scheduler to a real lifecycle @Override public void close() { scheduler.shutdownNow(); } } @ApplicationScoped class RatesLifecycle { @Inject FxRateRefresher refresher; @PreDestroy void stop() { refresher.close(); } }

steps.say: Self-check: a colleague suggests fun start() = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { ... } to avoid the opt-in warning. Why is that no better? (Each call makes a new root scope that nothing holds on to. Nobody can cancel it, so it leaks exactly like GlobalScope.)

lab.title: Stop leaking settlement work
steps: Run the tests. Five of seven fail. Read the messages: settleAll returns before anything is settled, and shutdown stops nothing.
Fix settleAll: replace GlobalScope with coroutineScope so every batch is a child of the call. The three settleAll tests should now pass.
In BatchSettler, add a private scope built from context + Job(), and make submit launch into it.
Write shutdown so it cancels the scope's job and waits for the children to stop. Make submit throw IllegalStateException once the scope is no longer active.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: coroutineScope { for (id in batchIds) launch { settle(id) } } is the whole fix for settleAll.
check(scope.isActive) { "settler is shut down" } throws IllegalStateException with that message. isActive on a scope comes from kotlinx.coroutines.isActive.
job is an extension property on CoroutineContext (import kotlinx.coroutines.job). cancelAndJoin() is an extension on Job.
The tests pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) as the context, so your scope runs on virtual time and shutdown returns at virtual time 0.

drill.title: An owned scope from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a class AuditWriter(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) with fun write(entry: String): Job that writes in the background, and suspend fun close() that cancels every pending write and waits until they have stopped. Use a suspend function persist(entry) that you can assume exists.

answer.html: class AuditWriter(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) { private val scope = CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job()) fun write(entry: String): Job = scope.launch { persist(entry) } suspend fun close() { scope.coroutineContext.job.cancelAndJoin() } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: the writer owns an executor and shuts it down class AuditWriter implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); Future<?> write(String entry) { return pool.submit(() -> persist(entry)); } @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupt pending writes pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // wait until they have stopped } }

recap: Every launch and async makes a child of the scope's job, so concurrent work forms a tree that mirrors the code.
A parent completes only after all of its children complete; coroutineScope returns after its slowest child.
A child failure cancels the parent and all siblings, then surfaces as one exception at the scope. Cancellation only travels down, and a CancellationException from a child does not alarm the parent.
GlobalScope (or a new CoroutineScope(...) inside a function) creates orphans: nothing waits for them, cancels them or sees their failures.
Work that outlives a call belongs to a class that owns a scope, launches into it, and cancels it at the end of its lifecycle.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to start a refund with GlobalScope.launch from a request handler, "so the response is fast". Explain what they lose, and what you would do instead.
explain.answer: A coroutine in GlobalScope has no parent, so it is outside the job tree. Nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it when the request is cancelled or the service shuts down, and if it fails, the exception goes to the uncaught handler instead of to anyone who can react. If the response really shouldn't wait for the refund, the refund needs a real owner: a component with its own scope that we cancel and join on shutdown. And because a refund must not be lost on a crash or a restart, the safest choice is to record it durably first (an outbox row or a Temporal workflow) and let a background worker with an owned scope process it.

deeper.html:
An owned scope does not have to be a separate root. Job(parent) creates a job that is a child of another one, so CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job(appJob)) gives you a component scope that is cancelled when the application job is cancelled. With a plain Job, the link also works upwards: a failure in the component cancels appJob too. That is usually not what you want for a long-lived component, which is one reason lesson 6 of this track reaches for SupervisorJob(parent).

The tree is also how kotlinx.coroutines reports problems. When several children fail, the first exception wins, and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. When you print a stack trace from a failed scope, look at the suppressed list before you conclude that only one thing went wrong.

The kotlinx-coroutines-debug module can dump the live coroutines of a running JVM with their states and creation stacks (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines()). It is not on this lab's classpath, but it is the tool to reach for when you suspect a leak in a real service. Without it, the cheap trick from the Try it, walking job.children from a known root, already tells you how much work a component still has in flight. Exposing inFlight per partition worker on a health or metrics endpoint is a cheap way to spot a stuck consumer.
